Question: If the proposition “\(a=0\)” is true, the negation of the proposition “For real values of \(a\) and \(b,\) if \(a=0,\) then \(ab=0\)” is:
Solution:
First read the conditional as a statement about fixed real numbers \(a,b\), with \(a=0\) assumed true as the stem says. Let \(P\) mean \(a=0\), and let \(Q\) mean \(ab=0\).

An implication \(P\Rightarrow Q\) is false exactly when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false. Its negation is therefore
\[
P\land\neg Q.
\]
Since \(P\) is assumed true, this reduces to \(\neg Q\), meaning \(ab\ne0\).

Choice C is \(P\Rightarrow\neg Q\). With \(P\) true, it also reduces to \(\neg Q\). But choice E is \(Q\Rightarrow\neg P\). Since \(\neg P\) is false, E is true exactly when \(Q\) is false, so it too reduces to \(\neg Q\). In fact, C and E are contrapositives and are logically equivalent. Without the assumption that \(P\) is true, neither is generally the negation \(P\land\neg Q\).

There is also a quantifier issue. If “for real values” means “for every real pair,” the negation of the whole statement is
\[
\text{There exist real }a,b\text{ such that }a=0\text{ and }ab\ne0.
\]
None of the choices explicitly states this existential claim.

Thus the item has no unique answer as written: under the stated true-antecedent reading, both \(\boxed{\text{C and E}}\) work.
